L38: Abstract
L39: A proxy re-encryption (PRE) scheme is a public-key encryption scheme that allows the holder of a key pk to derive a re-encryption key for any other key 𝑝𝑘′. This re-encryption key lets anyone transform ciphertexts under pk into ciphertexts under 𝑝𝑘′ without having to know the underlying message, while transformations from 𝑝𝑘′ to pk should not be possible (unidirectional).
L40: Security is defined in a multi-user setting against an adversary that gets the users’ public keys and can ask for re-encryption keys and can corrupt users by requesting their secret keys. Any ciphertext that the adversary cannot trivially decrypt given the obtained secret and re-encryption keys should be secure. All existing security proofs for PRE only show selective security, where the adversary must first declare the users it wants to corrupt.
L41: This can be lifted to more meaningful adaptive security by guessing the set of corrupted users among the n users, which loses a factor exponential in Open image in new window , rendering the result meaningless already for moderate Open image in new window . Jafargholi et al.
L42: (CRYPTO’17) proposed a framework that in some cases allows to give adaptive security proofs for schemes which were previously only known to be selectively secure, while avoiding the exponential loss that results from guessing the adaptive choices made by an adversary. We apply their framework to PREs that satisfy some natural additional properties. Concretely, we give a more fine-grained reduction for several unidirectional PREs, proving adaptive security at a much smaller loss.
L43: The loss depends on the graph of users whose edges represent the re-encryption keys queried by the adversary. For trees and chains the loss is quasi-polynomial in the size and for general graphs it is exponential in their depth and indegree (instead of their size as for previous reductions). Fortunately, trees and low-depth graphs cover many, if not most, interesting applications. Our results apply e.g. to the bilinear-map based PRE schemes by Ateniese et al.
L44: (NDSS’05 and CT-RSA’09), Gentry’s FHE-based scheme (STOC’09) and the LWE-based scheme by Chandran et al. (PKC’14).

L32: ## PUBLICATIONS
L33: 
L34:   1. Titan: Efficient Polynomial Commitments from IOPs over Groups
L35:     w/ Ravi Prakash, Samipa Samanta, Sruthi Sekar and Nitin Singh
L36:     CCS 2026, to appear
L37:     [+] Synopsis 【19†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【20†[↗]†github.com】 Code
L38:      * Problem: Polynomial Commitment Scheme (PCS) is a key ingredient to constructing efficient SNARKs. While hash-based PCSs (e.g., 【21†WHIR†ia.cr】) have low prover and verifier complexity, their proof size is usually large. On the other hand, pairing-based SNARKs (e.g., 【22†Dory†ia.cr】) have short proofs, but their prover and verifier complexity is high. Can we get a PCS that is the best of both worlds?
L39:      * Result: In this work, we propose Titan which achieves this.
L40:   2. Separating Verifiable Delay Functions and Time-Lock Puzzles
L41:     w/ Hamza Abusalah, Nivesh Aggarwal, Karen Azari, and Maximilian von Consbruch
L42:     Eurocrypt 2026
L43:     [+] Synopsis [↗] Paper 【23†[↓]】 Slides by Max and Nivesh 【24†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Max and Nivesh
L44:      * Problem: We continue with the problem posed in [26], where we showed that a weak form of VDF can be constructed from TLP using heavy machinery.
L45:      * Result: In this work, we show that (oracle-aided) VDFs cannot be constructed from TLPs and vice versa, and thus the limitations of [26] is inherent. To this end, we rely on the techniques from [27].
L46:   3. Impossibility of VDFs in the ROM: The Complete Picture
L47:     w/ Hamza Abusalah, Karen Azari, Erkan Tairi and Maximilian von Consbruch
L48:     Eurocrypt 2026
L49:     [+] Synopsis 【25†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【26†[↓]】 Slides 【27†[↓]】 Slides by Max 【28†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Max
L50:      * Problem: Can Verifiable Delay Function (VDF) be constructed in the 【29†Random-Oracle Model)†en.wikipedia.org】 (ROM)?
L51:      * Result: Prior works [【30†MSW20†ia.cr】,【31†GRY25†ia.cr】] ruled out ROM-based computationally-unique VDFs with public setup. We complete the picture set forth by these works by ruling out ROM-based computationally-unique VDFs even with expensive private setup.
L52:   4. On Verifiable Delay Functions from Time-Lock Puzzles
L53:     w/ Hamza Abusalah, Karen Azari, Dario Fiore and Erkan Tairi
L54:     PKC 2026
L55:     [+] Synopsis 【32†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【33†[↓]】 Slides by Erkan 【34†[↗]†pkc.iacr.org】 Talk by Erkan
L56:      * Problem: 【35†Time-Lock Puzzles (TLPs)†en.wikipedia.org】 and 【36†verifiable delay functions†cic.iacr.org】 (VDFs) are two central objects in timed cryptography. Constructions of TLP and VDF out there show superficial similarities: e.g., 【37†Pietrzak's†ia.cr】 and 【38†Wesolowski's†ia.cr】 constructions of VDF are essentially the 【39†Rivest-Shamir-Wagner†people.csail.mit.edu】 TLP made publicly-verifiable. This begs the natural question: can one object be constructed from the other in a black-box manner?
L57:      * Result: The problem turns out highly non-trivial! In this work, we are able to construct a one-time VDF from TLP, but using the heavy hammer of 【40†indistinguishability obfuscation.†en.wikipedia.org】
L58:   5. Securely Instantiating 'Half Gates' Garbling in the Standard Model
L59:     w/ Anasuya Acharya, Karen Azari, Mirza Ahad Baig and Dennis Hofheinz
L60:     PKC 2025
L61:     [+] Synopsis 【41†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【42†[↓]】 Slides by Anu 【43†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Anu
L62:      * Problem: The problem statement is related to that in [24]. Even though we showed that Half Gates cannot be adaptively secure in the plain model, can it be shown selective secure there? Prior results show selective security in idealised model, and this boils down constructing so-called "circular and correlation-robust" (CCR) hash function.
L63:      * Result: In this work, we show how to instantiate CCR hash function in the plain model using indistinguishability obfucation and injective one-way functions.
L64:   6. On the Adaptive Security of Free-XOR-based Garbling Schemes in the Plain Model
L65:     w/ Anasuya Acharya and Karen Azari
L66:     Eurocrypt 2025
L67:     [+] Synopsis 【44†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【45†[↓]】 Slides by Karen 【46†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Karen
L68:      * Problem: A common optimisation applied to Yao's 【47†garbling scheme†en.wikipedia.org】 is the so-called FreeXOR technique, which allows skipping the garbling table for XOR gates. While selective security of FreeXOR-based schemes is well-studied (e.g., 【48†here)†ia.cr】 in the plain model (i.e., no idealised assumptions), not much is known about its adaptive security (where the adversary gets to see a garbled circuit before choosing its input).
L69:      * Result: Building on [18], we show barriers against adaptive security of FreeXOR based schemes in the plain model. In particular, we show it is not possible to lift selective security of several popular schemes (such as 【49†Two Halves†ia.cr】 garbling) to adaptive security while avoiding an exponential loss in security.
L70:   7. Batch Proofs are Statistically Hiding
L71:     w/ Nir Bitansky, Omer Paneth, Ron Rothblum and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
L72:     STOC 2024
L73:     [+] Synopsis 【50†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【51†[↓]】 Slides 【52†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Prashant
L74:      * Problem: Given \(t\) instances of 【53†SAT†en.wikipedia.org】, the trivial way for an efficient prover to convince a verifier that all \(t\) instances are satisfiable is to send all the \(t\) satisfying assignments. Is it possible to do better in terms of communication? This is the problem of batch verification for \(\mathbf{NP}\).
L75:      * Result: We show (among other results) that this is unlikely by proving that such an interactive protocol can be used to construct a protocol that is (statistically) hides information about the assignments, which is believed to be unlikely.
L76:   8. (Verifiable) Delay Functions from Lucas Sequences
L77:     w/ Charlotte Hoffmann, Pavel Hubáček and Tomáš Krňák
L78:     TCC 2023
L79:     [+] Synopsis 【54†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【55†[↓]】 Slides by Tomáš 【56†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Tomáš
L80:      * Problem: A delay function is, loosely speaking, a function whose output cannot be computed faster even given parallelism. A verifiable delay function (VDF) is a delay function whose output can be "publicly certified" so that it can be verified by any party. Can we construct VDFs from weaker assumptions that those currently known?
L81:      * Result: We design (V)DFs assuming hardness of computing 【57†Lucas sequences†en.wikipedia.org】 in 【58†RSA group†en.wikipedia.org】. Furthermore, we conjecture that this assumption is a weaker than the 【39†Rivest-Shamir-Wagner†people.csail.mit.edu】 assumption, on which several current VDF candidates (【37†Pietrzak's†ia.cr】 and 【38†Wesolowski's†ia.cr】) are based on.
L82:   9. Certifying Giant Nonprimes
L83:     w/ Charlotte Hoffman, Pavel Hubáček and Krzysztof Pietrzak
L84:     PKC 2023
L85:     [+] Synopsis 【59†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【60†[↓]】 Slides by Charlotte 【61†[↗]†youtu.be】 Talk by Charlotte
L86:      * Problem: 【62†GIMPS†en.wikipedia.org】 and 【63†PrimeGrid†en.wikipedia.org】 are large-scale volunteer projects dedicated to searching giant prime numbers of special forms like 【64†Mersenne†en.wikipedia.org】 and 【65†Proth†en.wikipedia.org】 primes. The numbers in the current search-space are millions of digits large and a participating volunteer needs to run resource-consuming primality tests.
L87: Once a candidate prime \(N\) has been found, the only way for another party to independently verify the primality of \(N\) used to be by repeating the expensive primality test. Can we do better?
L88:      * Result: We propose a practical mechanism for certifying the non-primality of Proth numbers. That is, a volunteer can – parallel to running the primality test for \(N\) – generate an efficiently verifiable proof at a little extra cost certifying that \(N\) is not prime. The proof is obtained by applying the 【66†Fiat-Shamir heuristic†en.wikipedia.org】 to our interactive protocol, which has statistical soundness.
L89:   10. PPAD is as Hard as LWE and Iterated Squaring
L90:     w/ Nir Bitansky, Arka Rai Choudhuri, Justin Holmgren, Alex Lombardi, Omer Paneth and Ron Rothblum
L91:     TCC 2022
L92:     [+] Synopsis 【67†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【68†[↓]】 Slides 【69†[↗]†youtu.be】 Talk
L93:      * Problem: In [11,12], we showed hardness of the class 【70†\(\mathbf{PPAD}\)†en.wikipedia.org】 in the 【29†random-oracle model†en.wikipedia.org】 (additionally assuming worst-case hardness of 【71†\(\#\)SAT†en.wikipedia.org】). Follow-up works [【72†JKKZ20†ia.cr】,【73†LV20†ia.cr】] weakened the assumptions, but still rely on non-standard cryptographic assumptions. Is it possible to show \(\mathbf{PPAD}\)-hardness from polynomial hardness of standard cryptographic assumptions?
L94:      * Result: We use the recent results of Holmgren, Lombardi and Rothblum 【74†[HLR21]†ia.cr】 to derandomise the proof of exponentiation protocol of Block et al. 【75†[BHR+21]†ia.cr】, which yields hardness in \(\mathbf{PPAD}\) from polynomial hardness of iterated squaring (in any group) and 【76†learning with errors†en.wikipedia.org】. Furthermore, we strengthen this to show hardness of \(\mathbf{UEOPL}\subseteq\mathbf{PPAD}\), which is one of the lowest sub-classes of \(\mathbf{TFNP}\).
L95:   11. Practical Statistically-Sound Proofs of Exponentiation in Any Group
L96:     w/ Charlotte Hoffman, Pavel Hubáček, Karen Klein and Krzysztof Pietrzak
L97:     Crypto 2022
L98:     [+] Synopsis 【77†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【78†[↓]】 Slides by Charlotte 【79†[↗]†youtu.be】 Talk by Charlotte
L99:      * Problem: For a group \(\mathbb{G}\), a proof of exponentiation allows a prover to convince a verifier that \(y=x^{q^T}\) for \((y,x,q,T)\in\mathbb{G}^2\times\mathbb{N}^2\). The existing constructions are either impractical 【75†[BHK+12]†ia.cr】 or guarantee weak soundness [【37†Pie19†ia.cr】,【80†Wes20】]. Can we have the best of both worlds?
L100:      * Result: Building upon 【75†[BHK+12]†ia.cr】, we show that this is indeed possible for `structured' \(q\). Moreover, we show that for applications, such structured \(q\) suffices.
L101:   12. Limits on the Adaptive Security of Yao’s Garbling
L102:     w/ Karen Klein, Krzysztof Pietrzak and Daniel Wichs
L103:     Crypto 2021
L104:     [+] Synopsis 【81†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【82†[↓]】 Slides by Karen 【83†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk by Karen
L105:      * Problem: Can the upper bounds for loss in security of 【47†Yao's garbling†en.wikipedia.org】 shown in [7,18] improved?
L106:      * Result: We show that this is not possible using black-box reductions by building upon the result in [16]. As in [16], we use 【84†pebbling†en.wikipedia.org】 lower bounds and oracle separations.
L107:   13. On Treewidth, Separators and Yao’s Garbling
L108:     w/ Karen Klein and Krzysztof Pietrzak
L109:     TCC 2021
L110:     [+] Synopsis 【85†[↗]†ia.cr】 Paper 【86†[↓]】 Slides 【87†[↗]†www.youtube.com】 Talk
L111:      * Problem: In the 80s, Yao proposed an elegant way to 【88†securely evaluate functions†en.wikipedia.org】 using 【47†garbled circuits†en.wikipedia.org】. Is his garbling scheme fully secure?
L112:      * Result: Although security in a simulation-based model is known to be unattainable 【89†[AIKW13]†ia.cr】, we show that it is secure in the -- next-best -- indistinguishability-based model for some circuit classes. To this end, we use tools from algorithmic graph theory (e.g., 【90†treewidth†en.wikipedia.org】) and 【91†circuit complexity†en.wikipedia.org】
L113:   14. On the Cost of Adaptivity in Security Games on Graphs
